topic: Cognito user pools vs identity pools
question_text: A customer-facing GenAI web app needs to (1) sign users up and authenticate them, and (2) exchange the resulting tokens for temporary AWS credentials so the browser can call an API-Gateway-fronted Bedrock backend. Which Cognito components map to these two needs?

options.text: User Pools for sign-up/authentication; Identity Pools for exchanging tokens for temporary AWS credentials
Identity Pools for authentication; User Pools for AWS credentials
User Pools for both authentication and AWS credential vending
Neither — Cognito cannot issue AWS credentials

explanation: Cognito User Pools handle user directory, sign-up, and authentication (issuing JWT tokens); Cognito Identity Pools (federated identities) exchange those tokens for temporary, scoped AWS credentials via STS so the client can access AWS resources. The roles are distinct — User Pools authenticate, Identity Pools authorize AWS access — making the other options incorrect.
source_topic: Cognito User Pools vs Identity Pools

question_text: A regulated workload in a private VPC must call Amazon Bedrock without any traffic traversing the public internet. Which AWS capability provides this private connectivity?

options.text: An interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for Bedrock
An internet gateway with a public route
A NAT gateway to the public Bedrock endpoint
Amazon CloudFront in front of Bedrock

explanation: An interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink gives private, in-VPC connectivity to Bedrock so traffic never leaves the AWS network. An internet gateway and a NAT gateway both route to the public internet; CloudFront is a CDN and does not create private VPC connectivity to Bedrock.
source_topic: PrivateLink interface VPC endpoint for Bedrock

question_text: For the subnet and instances hosting a self-managed GenAI inference service, a team must apply STATEFUL instance-level filtering and separately a STATELESS subnet-level control. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Security Groups = stateful, instance-level; Network ACLs = stateless, subnet-level
Security Groups = stateless, subnet-level; Network ACLs = stateful, instance-level
Both are stateful and operate at the subnet level
Both are stateless and operate at the instance level

explanation: Security Groups are stateful (return traffic is automatically allowed) and act at the instance/ENI level; Network ACLs are stateless (you must allow both directions explicitly) and act at the subnet level. The other options invert or conflate these properties.

topic: Protecting public GenAI endpoints with WAF and Shield
question_text: A public-facing GenAI API endpoint must be protected from common web exploits and application-layer abuse (e.g. injection patterns, rate-based flooding) at the edge. Which AWS service provides these configurable Layer-7 protections?

options.text: AWS WAF with managed and rate-based rules
AWS KMS
Amazon Macie
AWS Secrets Manager

explanation: AWS WAF inspects HTTP(S) requests at Layer 7 and enforces managed rule groups and rate-based rules to block common exploits and abusive traffic on API Gateway/CloudFront/ALB-fronted endpoints. KMS manages encryption keys, Macie discovers sensitive data in S3, and Secrets Manager stores secrets — none provide Layer-7 request filtering.
source_topic: AWS WAF for public GenAI endpoint protection

question_text: Which AWS service is specifically designed to protect internet-facing GenAI endpoints against distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, with an Advanced tier offering enhanced mitigations and cost protection?

options.text: AWS Shield (Standard and Advanced)
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Config
Amazon Inspector

explanation: AWS Shield provides managed DDoS protection; Shield Standard is automatic, and Shield Advanced adds enhanced mitigations, 24/7 response, and cost protection. GuardDuty is threat detection, AWS Config tracks resource configuration/compliance, and Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities — none are dedicated DDoS mitigation services.
